body.text: In short:
Anthropic's market value has blown past $US2.1 trillion ($3.1 trillion) in its Nasdaq debut, higher than SpaceX's June listing.
CEO Dario Amodei and six co-founders, who together own about 10 per cent of the frontier AI firm, have stakes now valued at around $US225 billion combined.
What's next:
Investors are watching whether the AI company's enormous valuation can be sustained amid growing concerns about the AI sector.
Shares in Anthropic have surged in their Wall Street debut, briefly pushing the artificial intelligence company's market value above $US2 trillion ($3 trillion), overtaking SpaceX's debut.

The maker of the Claude AI chatbot opened at $US111.50 ($167) on the Nasdaq, a 34 per cent jump from its initial public offering price of $US83, as investors rushed to buy into the first major frontier AI company to list on a stock exchange.
The debut marked a major milestone for the AI industry, but the initial excitement faded as investors took profits and its shares gave up some of the early gains.
The main US indexes also retreated amid renewed jitters over the sector's outlook. The stock, trading under the ticker ANT, was last quoted at $US96.30, as at 7am AEDT.
Anthropic raised $US81.3 billion through its IPO, alongside a further $US26 billion in a concurrent private placement involving major technology companies.

The listing comes at a turbulent time for the technology sector, which has been rattled by concerns of an AI bubble, worries over mounting debt among data centre operators and a widening scandal that forced Nvidia founder Jensen Huang to step down as CEO.
Jun Bei Liu, founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap, said she had expected Anthropic's debut to help revive enthusiasm for AI stocks, but that had failed to materialise.
"I think tomorrow you will probably see the stock dropping in the red, there certainly seems like there's enough demand, but the price is still too high."
Australians offered access to record IPO
Australian investors were among a select group outside the United States given the opportunity to buy shares in Anthropic before its stock market debut.
Commonwealth Bank-owned CommSec was appointed the lead Australian retail broker, with investors also able to apply through participating brokers including Stake and Sharesies.
CommBank also stands to benefit from Anthropic's success, having invested in the AI company in 2025.
According to its latest annual report, the value of CBA's stake had climbed to $1.53 billion by the end of June, up from $153 million a year earlier.
CommSec and Sharesies declined to comment when asked about demand among Australian retail investors.
Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said his firm's grey market indicators had pointed to a strong debut for Anthropic.
The indicator allows traders to speculate on a company's share price before it officially hits the stock exchange, providing an early indication of investor expectations.
"If you sort of use that as a rough guide, demand's been really strong," he said.
Mr Rodda compared the excitement to the launch of a new iPhone.
"People lining up around the streets to be some of the first people to get their hands on it," he said.
"It's very, very much a similar sort of psychology dynamic amongst investors."
Ms Liu from Ten Cap said strong demand for Anthropic shares was partly due to their limited availability, with relatively few shares being offered to investors.
Valuation questions remain
Ms Liu believes Anthropic is a "great company" but has decided against buying shares at the current valuation.
"It's just too expensive," she said.
"It's yet to make money so you're paying a lot for a company based on what they can achieve, they still need to get there.
"Remember, they still have to achieve it."
She said the company's shares would start to look very attractive to her if its share price fell about 20–30 per cent from listing price.

Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers, Anthropic has experienced explosive growth, with revenue surging 13-fold to $US33.2 billion in the first nine months of this year, driven largely by businesses adopting its AI products, particularly Claude Code.
But despite this, Anthropic is still losing money, reporting an operating loss of $US1.26 billion over the same period, highlighting the enormous costs of developing and running advanced AI models.

The company also faces significant costs as it expands, with around $US900 billion in long-term spending commitments, largely tied to computing power and infrastructure needed to develop as well as run its AI models.
Investors are also buying into a company where the seven co-founders will retain a majority (50.1 per cent) of shareholder voting power, limiting the influence of shareholders over major decisions.
Daniel Newman, chief executive of US technology research firm Futurum Group, said the broader AI industry still faced some difficult questions despite Anthropic's record float.
He pointed to high interest rates, persistent inflation and geopolitical uncertainty weighing on technology stocks, even as demand for AI continues to grow.
"Nvidia's strong earnings didn't save the AI trade. Anthropic's IPO probably won't save it either," he said.
